bibl.title: A Long-Term Analysis of Polarization on Twitter

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: existence
span.quote: Our analysis shows that online polarization has indeed increased over the past eight years and that, depending on the measure, the relative change is 10%-20%.

span.label: political polarization on Twitter
span.quote: In this paper, we try to answer the question of whether political polarization in the US on Twitter has increased over the last eight years.

span.label: observational-data-analysis
span.quote: We analyze a large longitudinal Twitter dataset of 679,000 users and look at signs of polarization in their (i) network - how people follow political and media accounts, (ii) tweeting behavior - whether they retweet content from both sides, and (iii) content - how partisan the hashtags they use are.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the time a user began following is ESTIMATED, from the reverse-chronological order the API returns followers in, lower-bounded by each follower's account creation date
span.quote: This method is based on the fact that the Twitter API returns followers in the reverse chronological order in which they followed and we can lower bound the follow time using the account creation date of a user. So, as at least some of @BarackObama’s followers started to follow him right after creating their Twitter account, this leads to temporal bounds for the other followers as well.

span.label: the paper's REASON for the Bayesian treatment - that a single act from one side is a weak signal - is the sentence immediately before this one, and widening to reach it pulls in a footnote the extraction has interleaved into the body ('4Since the Twitter API restricts us to the last 3200 tweets'), so the tag is trimmed instead
span.term: each user's leaning is a beta-binomial coin-bias estimate - a uniform prior over the two sides, then one increment per follow or retweet
span.quote: Before observing any evidence, we gave each following (retweeting) user a uniform prior probability to follow (retweet) seed users from either side. Concretely, we used a beta distribution with a uniform prior (α = β = 1), where α measures the left leaning and β the right leaning. Then every follow (retweet) to either side increases the count for that side by +1, basically simulating a repeated coin toss where we are studying the bias of the coin.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: polarization is defined as DISTANCE FROM BALANCE rather than as leaning, so a strongly left and a strongly right user score identically
span.quote: We defined the polarization p as p = 2 · |0.5 − l|, giving a measure between 0.0 and 1.0 measuring the deviation from a balanced leaning.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: a hashtag inherits its leaning from the users who used it that week, and users who did not retweet a seed account that week contribute nothing
span.quote: a given week, a user is assigned a leaning based on the political seed accounts they retweet during that week. Users not retweeting seed accounts during the week do not contribute. Each hashtag h is then assigned a leaning lh between 0.0=right and 1.0=left based on the leaning of the users using the hashtags in the given week. Differences in user volumes for the two sides are corrected for and smoothing is applied to deal with sparsity.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: two explicit noise controls chosen because the early years are thin: a minimum of five users per hashtag, and a five-week moving average
span.quote: To further reduce noise due to low volumes, in particular during the early years, we (i) ignored hashtags used by fewer than five users, and (ii) computed moving averages across five weeks.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: automated and bad-faith accounts are handled BY THE PASSAGE OF TIME rather than by detection - the study relies on Twitter having suspended them in the years before collection
span.quote: However, due to the longitudinal nature of our study, by the time of the data collection (2016/2017) Twitter will have had time to catch most cases of users violating their terms of service, suspending their accounts.

span.label: Twitter API 'most recent activity only' limitations hinder longitudinal study
span.note: what this limits: any longitudinal claim: API LIMITATIONS HINDER SUCH STUDIES - only most-recent activity is retrievable
span.quote: API limitations hinder such studies

span.label: Automated tweets and astroturfing were not detected or removed.
span.note: what this limits: the authenticity of the measured activity: WE DID NOT EXPLICITLY ATTEMPT TO DETECT ASTROTURFING AND OTHER TYPES OF AUTOMATED TWEETS
span.quote: In our work, we did not explicitly attempt to detect “astroturfing” and other types of automated tweets [13].

span.label: Hashtag hijacking could still contaminate the content measure.
span.note: what this limits: the content measure, with the boundary decision stated: HASHTAG HIJACKING COULD STILL AFFECT OUR ANALYSIS, THOUGH THESE EFFECTS ARE ARGUABLY ALSO PART OF THE POLITICAL LANDSCAPE AND SHOULD BE INCLUDED
span.quote: More organic efforts such as hashtag hijacking [8] could still affect our analysis, though these effects are arguably also part of the political landscape and should be included.

span.label: The study cannot settle whether social media causes, reflects or reduces offline polarization.
span.note: what this limits: any causal reading: the study cannot settle whether social media causes, reflects or reduces offline polarization
span.quote: Though our analysis does not directly settle this debate, it provides evidence that polarization on Twitter has increased over the past eight years, potentially reflecting increases in offline polarization as those observed in the US House of Representatives [2].

span.label: The election-period pattern in hashtag polarization does not hold for the 2010 midterms, probably because of noisier early estimates.
span.note: what this limits: the election-period pattern: FOR THE 2010 MIDTERM ELECTIONS, HOWEVER, THIS OBSERVATION DOES NOT HOLD, POTENTIALLY DUE TO NOISIER ESTIMATES BASED ON FEWER ACTIVE USERS
span.quote: For the 2010 midterm elections, however, this observation does not hold, potentially due to noisier estimates based on fewer active users on Twitter.

span.label: Pre-September-2009 tweets were excluded because their volume was too low.
span.note: what this limits: the temporal coverage of the analysis: WE ONLY CONSIDER TWEETS FROM SEPTEMBER 2009 ONWARDS ... SINCE THE VOLUME FOR EARLIER TWEETS IS LOW
span.quote: Though we have tweets dating back to 2007, we only consider tweets from September 2009 onwards in the analysis since the volume for earlier tweets is low.

span.label: The follow times underlying the whole time series are estimated rather than observed, and the accuracy attributed to that estimator is reported second-hand and only for accounts with millions of followers.
span.note: what this limits: the year-by-year following curve: follow dates are estimated by the method of Meeder et al., whose accuracy is reported to hold for users with millions of followers, while the analysis uses all cases with estimated follow dates from January 2009 onwards
span.quote: estimates are reported to be fairly accurate when estimating follow times for users with millions of followers. For our analysis, we used all cases with estimated follow dates from January 2009 onwards

span.label: The content measure is not specified in this paper; its method is applied from another work and the reader is sent there for the details.
span.note: what this limits: the hashtag-polarization series: the procedure that produces it - leaning assignment, volume correction and smoothing - is taken from another paper, and this one refers the reader there for details
span.quote: We operationalize this idea by applying the methodology previously used in [15]. In their methodology, for a given week, a user is assigned a leaning based on the political seed accounts they retweet during that week. Users not retweeting seed accounts during the week do not contribute. Each hashtag h is then assigned a leaning lh between 0.0=right and 1.0=left based on the leaning of the users using the hashtags in the given week. Differences in user volumes for the two sides are corrected for and smoothing is applied to deal with sparsity. For each hashtag h in a given week, its polarization ph is then, as before, defined as ph = 2 · |0.5 − l|. The values of ph are then averaged across all h used in a given week by retweeting users. See

span.label: Each user's polarization value is a posterior belief that begins from an assumed balance between the two sides, not a summary of that user's observed behaviour alone.
span.note: what this limits: a per-user polarization value: it is the mean of a beta posterior that starts from a uniform prior over left and right and is updated by each observed follow or retweet, so a user with few observed actions is scored largely by the prior
span.quote: Before observing any evidence, we gave each following (retweeting) user a uniform prior probability to follow (retweet) seed users from either side

span.label: social-network-structure analysis applied to measure political polarization on Twitter
span.quote: we collect data from Twitter related to both social network structure and tweet content for a large set of users (679,000) engaging with US politics

span.label: three separate questions, each answered from A DIFFERENT TYPE OF INFORMATION, rather than one measure carried through
span.quote: To avoid drawing conclusions based on a single perspective, we address three questions each using a different type of information.

span.quote: We define polarization as a tendency to be restricted in terms of obtaining or engaging with political information to one side of the left-vs.-right political spectrum

span.label: polarization - AS A NUMBER: twice the absolute deviation of a beta-posterior leaning from 0.5, so it measures distance from a balanced diet on a 0.0 to 1.0 scale and nothing else
span.quote: We defined the polarization p as p = 2 · |0.5 − l|, giving a measure between 0.0 and 1.0 measuring the deviation from a balanced leaning

span.label: polarization - AS LEXICAL DIVERGENCE: two sides that describe the same thing in completely different words, the paper's own example being global warming versus climategate
span.quote: Conceptually, a society could be thought of as polarized if there are two opposing sides who speak different languages, in that they differ completely in the words they choose to describe things. For example, one person’s “global warming” could be another person

span.label: the term's scope - FIXED BY STIPULATION IN A FOOTNOTE: every later use of the bare word is declared to mean political polarization
